title: Low, medium and geostationary orbits compared
examples: Why don't satellite dishes need to move?

explain.say: Satellites orbit at very different heights depending on their job. The higher the orbit, the slower a satellite moves and the longer one lap takes.

draw.text: Low, medium and geostationary orbits compared

explain.say: Low Earth orbit, a few hundred kilometres up, is home to the space station and internet satellites. They race round in about 90 minutes, close enough for sharp photos and quick signals.
GPS satellites fly in medium orbit, about 20,000 kilometres up, each lap taking about 12 hours. From that height each one can see a large part of Earth.

At about 35,800 kilometres, one lap takes exactly one day, the time Earth takes to spin. A satellite above the equator there seems to hang still in the sky, so TV dishes can point at it and never move.

faq.a: It is an orbit about 35,800 kilometres above the equator where a satellite takes exactly one day to go round, matching Earth's spin. From the ground it seems to stay in one spot, ideal for TV and weather satellites.
asks: Why do satellite dishes not move?

faq.q: Why do low satellites go faster?
faq.a: Gravity is stronger closer to Earth, so a low satellite must go faster sideways to avoid falling in. The space station travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour; geostationary satellites at about 11,000.

faq.q: What is low Earth orbit used for?
faq.a: Low Earth orbit, up to about 2,000 kilometres, holds the space station, Earth-imaging satellites and internet constellations like Starlink. Being close gives sharp pictures and fast signals, but each satellite sees only a small patch at a time.

faq.q: Why are GPS satellites in medium orbit?
faq.a: At about 20,200 kilometres each GPS satellite sees a large part of Earth, so a couple of dozen of them are enough to keep at least four in view from anywhere on the planet.
A polar orbit passes over or near the North and South Poles. As Earth spins underneath, the satellite eventually passes over every part of the planet, which is handy for mapping and weather.
asks: Why do some satellites go over the poles?

facts: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometres up and circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Geostationary satellites orbit about 35,786 kilometres above the equator.
Arthur C. Clarke popularised the idea of geostationary communication satellites in 1945.
